content:
Yesterday brought two contrasting reports about next year's iPhone; the device, seen as the iPhone's twentieth anniversary model, is also described as the concrete realisation of Apple's long-standing 'a single sheet of glass' vision.

As for what we can actually expect, reports have been contradictory for some time, but yesterday's divergence was arguably the most dramatic so far…

Current situation

Former Apple design chief Jony Ive has often spoken of his long-term vision of ultimately turning the iPhone into 'a single sheet of glass'; even though Ive has left the company, the prevailing view remains that Apple has been steadily moving in that direction.

Although Apple generally doesn't make a big fuss over anniversaries, the consensus is that they want to get as close as possible to realising this vision before the iPhone's twentieth anniversary. This could include embedding Face ID under the display and hiding the front-facing camera beneath the screen.

However, we have already seen conflicting reports on these expectations. The original view was that this would be a standalone model, similar to the iPhone Air and the upcoming iPhone Ultra, but more recent reports have pointed to the design appearing on next year's iPhone Pro models.

In terms of naming, this would be called the iPhone 19 Pro, but Apple could also choose to skip a generation and name it the iPhone 20 to mark the anniversary.

Yesterday's conflicting reports

Yesterday's situation was further muddied when an analyst claimed Apple had abandoned plans for an all-glass iPhone next year.

But Mark Gurman of Bloomberg quickly pushed back on that claim.

What is more likely to be the case

The point is that Apple's vision for the iPhone doesn't have a single, final destination. What they plan to launch next year is just one step—or several steps—towards that science-fiction-inspired 'single sheet of glass' vision.

The question isn't whether that goal can be achieved next year, but how far Apple will go in that direction. But whether it's one step or several, it absolutely won't be the last step in the iPhone's design evolution.

In fact, Gurman revealed that Apple has actually scaled back some of what was previously expected for next year.

Analysts at Jefferies most likely received the same information, just a beat slower, and mistakenly assumed the whole plan had been shelved.

My personal expectation is that next year's design will be a major leap forward—comparable to the breakthrough of the iPhone X—but with further developments still to come in the years ahead. For me, the biggest question is whether the 2027 iPhone will have a breakthrough large enough to be worth marking in some special way, such as being labelled a twentieth-anniversary iPhone (which I think is unlikely), being given a special name, or skipping a generation to be called the iPhone 20.

What are your expectations? Feel free to share your views in the comments section.
